Session fixation; regenerate the session ID at login

explanation.correct: Session fixation plants a known session identifier so it is already valid after the victim logs in; issuing a fresh session ID upon authentication defeats it.

distractors.A: This is fixation, not sniffing, and disabling ICMP does nothing to protect session IDs.
distractors.B: XSS can steal tokens but is a different attack; adding RAM is irrelevant to it.
distractors.C: The victim already authenticates legitimately, so this is not brute force of a password.

explanation.exam_pattern: Pre-set a session ID reused after login = session fixation (regenerate ID at login).

questions.stem: Which TWO cookie attributes most directly protect a session cookie from being stolen by client-side script and from being sent over an unencrypted HTTP connection? (Choose two.)

explanation.correct: HttpOnly blocks JavaScript from reading the cookie (mitigating XSS theft), and Secure ensures the cookie is only sent over HTTPS, so it is not exposed on plaintext HTTP.

distractors.A: Domain scopes which hosts receive the cookie; it does not stop script access or plaintext exposure.
distractors.B: Max-Age sets the cookie's lifetime; it does not protect it from script theft or HTTP transmission.

explanation.exam_pattern: Protect a session cookie = HttpOnly (no script) + Secure (HTTPS only); SameSite adds CSRF defense.

questions.stem: An IDS that learns a baseline of normal behavior and flags deviations from it can catch previously unknown attacks, at the cost of more false positives. Which detection method is this?

explanation.correct: Anomaly (behavior) based detection compares activity to a learned baseline, so it can detect novel/zero-day attacks but produces more false positives than signature matching.

distractors.A: A honeypot is a decoy host, not an IDS detection method.
distractors.C: Signature-based detection matches known patterns and misses novel attacks it has no signature for.
distractors.D: Stateful inspection tracks connection state in a firewall; it is not baseline-deviation detection.

explanation.exam_pattern: Baseline deviation, catches unknown attacks, more false positives = anomaly-based detection.

references: CEH v13 Module 12: Evading IDS, Firewalls, and Honeypots

questions.stem: Which intrusion-detection sensor is installed on an individual endpoint and watches that host's own logs, file integrity, and processes rather than network traffic?

explanation.correct: A host-based IDS runs on the endpoint and monitors local activity (logs, file changes, processes), seeing things a network sensor cannot, such as host-local or encrypted-then-decrypted activity.

distractors.A: A NIDS monitors traffic on a network segment, not a single host's internal logs and files.
distractors.B: A proxy firewall mediates connections at the application layer; it is not an endpoint IDS.
distractors.D: A load balancer distributes traffic; it is not an intrusion-detection sensor.

explanation.exam_pattern: Sensor on the endpoint watching local logs/files/processes = HIDS; on the wire = NIDS.

references: CEH v13 Module 12: Evading IDS, Firewalls, and Honeypots

questions.stem: Which firewall type tracks the state of active connections so it can automatically permit the return traffic of a session it already allowed, instead of judging each packet in isolation?

explanation.correct: A stateful inspection firewall maintains a connection/state table, so return packets of an established, permitted session are allowed without a separate inbound rule.

distractors.A: A repeater regenerates signals on a segment; it is not a firewall.
distractors.B: A hub repeats frames to all ports; it performs no filtering at all.
distractors.D: A stateless packet filter evaluates each packet independently and keeps no connection state.

explanation.exam_pattern: Tracks connection state to allow return traffic = stateful inspection firewall.

references: CEH v13 Module 12: Evading IDS, Firewalls, and Honeypots

questions.stem: To slip past a firewall rule that only trusts a specific internal source address, an attacker forges the source IP of their packets to impersonate that trusted host. Which technique is this?

explanation.correct: IP spoofing forges the source address to masquerade as a trusted host, defeating source-based ACLs; ingress/egress filtering (e.g., BCP 38) is a core defense.

distractors.A: Tunneling hides traffic inside an allowed protocol; it is not source-address forgery.
distractors.B: Fragmentation splits packets to confuse reassembly; it does not spoof the source address.
distractors.D: Encoding obfuscates the payload to dodge signatures; it does not impersonate a trusted source IP.

explanation.exam_pattern: Forge the source IP to impersonate a trusted host = IP spoofing (ingress filtering defends).

references: CEH v13 Module 12: Evading IDS, Firewalls, and Honeypots

questions.stem: Which TWO are legitimate defensive benefits of deploying a honeypot? (Choose two.)

options.text: It removes the need to patch production systems
It can divert attackers away from real production systems
It serves as the organization's primary production database
It detects and studies attacker techniques with very few false positives

explanation.correct: A honeypot has no production use, so almost any interaction is suspicious (low false positives), and it can lure and delay attackers away from real assets while defenders observe their methods.

distractors.A: Honeypots aid detection and research; they never replace patching real systems.
distractors.C: A honeypot must hold no real production data; using it as a production database defeats its purpose and is dangerous.

explanation.exam_pattern: Honeypot value = low-false-positive detection + diversion/study; never production data or a patch substitute.

references: CEH v13 Module 12: Evading IDS, Firewalls, and Honeypots

questions.stem: Attackers alter the visual content of an organization's public home page to display their own message, primarily to embarrass the victim and damage its reputation. Which web-server attack is this?

explanation.correct: Website defacement replaces or modifies the site's visible content to push the attacker's message, usually for notoriety or hacktivism, harming the owner's reputation.

distractors.A: A denial-of-service makes the site unavailable; it does not rewrite the page's content.
distractors.B: Directory traversal reads files outside the web root; it is not about changing the home page's appearance.
distractors.C: SQL injection manipulates database queries; defacement is about altering displayed content.

explanation.exam_pattern: Replace the visible page to send a message = website defacement.

references: CEH v13 Module 13: Hacking Web Servers

questions.stem: Which TWO HTTP methods, if left unnecessarily enabled on a web server, can let an attacker upload or delete files on the server? (Choose two.)

explanation.correct: PUT can write/upload a file and DELETE can remove one; if these methods are enabled without strict controls, an attacker may place a web shell or destroy content. Disable unneeded methods.

distractors.A: HEAD returns only headers (no body); it is low-risk and does not modify files.
distractors.D: GET retrieves a resource; it is a standard, expected read method, not a file-write primitive.

explanation.exam_pattern: Risky write methods to disable = PUT/DELETE; GET/HEAD are normal read methods.

references: CEH v13 Module 13: Hacking Web Servers

questions.stem: Requesting a folder with no index page, an attacker receives the server's full list of files and subfolders, revealing scripts and backups. Which misconfiguration caused this?

explanation.correct: When directory listing/browsing is enabled and no index file exists, the server returns the folder's contents, leaking structure and files; disable auto-indexing to fix it.

distractors.A: XSS runs script in a victim's browser; it does not enumerate server folders.
distractors.C: Directory traversal uses ../ sequences to escape the web root; here the server simply lists a folder it serves.
distractors.D: Default admin credentials are a login weakness, not the cause of an exposed file listing.

explanation.exam_pattern: Server lists folder contents when no index page = directory listing/browsing enabled.

references: CEH v13 Module 13: Hacking Web Servers

questions.stem: A web application returns detailed stack traces and raw database error text to end users. Beyond being untidy, why is this a security concern?

options.text: It is information disclosure that helps attackers fingerprint and target the stack
It forces all users to use HTTPS
It encrypts traffic too strongly for clients
It is a denial-of-service against the database

explanation.correct: Verbose errors leak internal details (software versions, file paths, SQL structure) - information disclosure that lets an attacker tailor further attacks. Return generic error pages instead.

distractors.B: Showing errors does not force HTTPS; it exposes internals over whatever transport is used.
distractors.C: Verbose errors have nothing to do with encryption strength.
distractors.D: Leaking error text is disclosure, not a denial-of-service on the database.

explanation.exam_pattern: Detailed stack traces/DB errors to users = information disclosure (use generic error pages).

references: CEH v13 Module 13: Hacking Web Servers

questions.stem: Fill in the blank: Hardening a web server by removing sample applications, default accounts, and unused modules shrinks its attack ______, giving an attacker fewer things to target.

explanation.correct: Reducing the attack surface - the sum of exposed features and entry points - by stripping samples, defaults, and unused components is a foundational web-server hardening practice.
explanation.exam_pattern: Remove samples/defaults/unused modules to shrink the attack = surface.

references: CEH v13 Module 13: Hacking Web Servers

questions.stem: An attacker abuses a vulnerable feature to make the server itself fetch a URL of the attacker's choosing, reaching internal-only services or a cloud metadata endpoint. Which OWASP Top 10 attack is this?

explanation.correct: SSRF tricks the server into making attacker-chosen requests, so it can reach internal systems or cloud metadata that the attacker cannot hit directly; allow-list outbound destinations to defend.

distractors.A: CSRF makes the victim's browser (not the server) send a forged request using the user's session.
distractors.C: IDOR reaches other users' objects via reference tampering; it is not server-side URL fetching.
distractors.D: Reflected XSS runs script in the victim's browser; it does not make the server fetch URLs.

explanation.exam_pattern: Make the SERVER fetch an attacker URL (internal/metadata) = SSRF; browser-side forged request = CSRF.

references: CEH v13 Module 14: Hacking Web Applications

questions.stem: A web form passes user input unsanitized into a server-side operating-system shell call, letting an attacker run arbitrary system commands on the host. Which vulnerability class is this?

explanation.correct: Command injection occurs when untrusted input is concatenated into an OS command, so the attacker executes system commands; avoid shelling out and use safe APIs with strict input validation.

distractors.A: Directory traversal reads files via path manipulation; it does not execute OS commands.
distractors.B: SQL injection alters database queries, not OS shell commands.
distractors.C: XSS runs script in the browser; command injection runs commands on the server OS.

explanation.exam_pattern: Untrusted input into an OS shell call = command injection (runs system commands).

references: CEH v13 Module 14: Hacking Web Applications

questions.stem: A 'page=' parameter lets an attacker make the application load and execute a script hosted on the attacker's own remote server. Which attack is this, specifically?

explanation.correct: Remote File Inclusion makes the app include and run a file fetched from a remote (attacker) URL, often leading to code execution; disable remote includes and validate the parameter.

distractors.B: Clickjacking tricks a user into clicking a hidden element; it does not include remote files.
distractors.C: LFI includes a file already present on the local server, not one fetched from a remote URL.
distractors.D: Reflected XSS executes script in the browser, not a server-side remote include.

explanation.exam_pattern: Include/execute a file from a REMOTE URL = RFI; from the LOCAL server = LFI.

references: CEH v13 Module 14: Hacking Web Applications

questions.stem: A web app parses attacker-supplied XML that declares an external entity pointing at a local server file, causing the parser to read and return that file's contents. Which attack is this?

explanation.correct: XXE abuses an XML parser that resolves external entities, letting an attacker read local files or reach internal systems; disable external entity/DTD processing to prevent it.

distractors.A: Clickjacking manipulates UI layering; it does not involve XML external entities.
distractors.B: CSRF forces a state-changing request via the victim's session; it is not XML parsing abuse.
distractors.C: SQL injection targets database queries, not XML entity resolution.

explanation.exam_pattern: Malicious XML external entity reading server files = XXE (disable external entities).

references: CEH v13 Module 14: Hacking Web Applications

questions.stem: An attacker overlays an invisible frame of a target site on top of harmless-looking decoy content so the victim's clicks are hijacked into actions on the target. Which header best defends this?

options.text: User-Agent - the attack is ARP poisoning
Accept-Encoding - the attack is a SYN flood
X-Frame-Options (or CSP frame-ancestors) - the attack is clickjacking
Content-Length - the attack is SQL injection

explanation.correct: Clickjacking frames the target invisibly to steal clicks; X-Frame-Options or the CSP frame-ancestors directive tells browsers to refuse framing the page, defeating it.

distractors.A: User-Agent identifies the client; ARP poisoning is a LAN attack unrelated to framing.
distractors.B: Accept-Encoding negotiates compression; a SYN flood is a network DoS, not a framing attack.
distractors.D: Content-Length is a size header and does not defend against clickjacking; SQLi is unrelated here.

explanation.exam_pattern: Invisible frame stealing clicks = clickjacking; defend with X-Frame-Options / CSP frame-ancestors.

references: CEH v13 Module 14: Hacking Web Applications

questions.stem: An application rebuilds objects from untrusted serialized data without validating it, letting a crafted object trigger remote code execution. Which flaw is this?

explanation.correct: Insecure deserialization trusts attacker-controlled serialized data; a malicious object can execute code or tamper with logic. Validate/sign serialized data or avoid native deserialization.

distractors.B: Broken access control is about missing authorization checks, not reconstructing malicious objects.
distractors.C: Security misconfiguration covers insecure settings/defaults, a different root cause.
distractors.D: SQL injection manipulates queries; it is not object deserialization.

explanation.exam_pattern: Rebuild untrusted serialized objects -> code execution = insecure deserialization.

references: CEH v13 Module 14: Hacking Web Applications

questions.stem: Malicious input is safely stored on first submission but is later used unsafely by a different query, so the injection fires during a subsequent operation rather than at input time. Which SQLi type?

explanation.correct: Second-order SQL injection stores tainted input that a later, different query executes unsafely, so the payload triggers on a subsequent action - harder to spot in testing.

distractors.A: 'Reflected' is an XSS concept; classic in-band SQLi fires on the same request, not later.
distractors.C: UNION-based injection returns data directly in the immediate response (in-band).
distractors.D: Error-based injection leaks data through database error messages in the same response.

explanation.exam_pattern: Stored input exploited by a LATER query = second-order (stored) SQL injection.

questions.stem: When results cannot be returned in the HTTP response, an attacker makes the database send the stolen data to an attacker-controlled server over DNS or HTTP. Which SQL injection category is this?

explanation.correct: Out-of-band SQLi exfiltrates data through a separate channel (DNS/HTTP callbacks) when the app does not return results or respond timingly in-band - useful against blind, quiet endpoints.

distractors.B: Boolean-based blind infers data from true/false response differences, still in the same channel.
distractors.C: UNION-based returns data directly in the response (in-band).
distractors.D: In-band SQLi returns data in the same response channel, the opposite of out-of-band.

explanation.exam_pattern: Exfiltrate via a separate channel (DNS/HTTP) = out-of-band SQL injection.

questions.stem: Beyond using parameterized queries, which configuration most limits the damage of a successful SQL injection by ensuring the application's database account cannot drop tables or read system data?

options.text: Grant the app's database account only least-privilege permissions

explanation.correct: Running the application under a least-privilege database account means even a successful injection cannot drop tables or reach system catalogs, containing the blast radius (defense in depth).

distractors.A: User password length does not constrain the database account's privileges.
distractors.C: Client-side limits are trivially bypassed by sending requests directly to the server.
distractors.D: Hiding the banner is obscurity; it does not limit what a successful injection can do.

explanation.exam_pattern: Limit SQLi blast radius = least-privilege DB account (plus parameterized queries).

questions.stem: Which control inspects incoming HTTP requests for malicious patterns such as SQL injection and XSS and can block them before they reach the application, acting as a compensating defense?

explanation.correct: A WAF inspects HTTP(S) request content at the application layer and can block SQLi/XSS patterns, serving as a compensating control while code is fixed (not a replacement for secure coding).

distractors.B: A DNS resolver maps names to IPs; it has no role in blocking web-app attacks.
distractors.C: A network firewall filters by port/IP/state; it does not parse HTTP payloads for SQLi/XSS.
distractors.D: A load balancer distributes traffic; it does not inspect for web-attack payloads.

explanation.exam_pattern: Inspect/block SQLi/XSS in HTTP requests = Web Application Firewall (WAF).

questions.stem: Fill in the blank: A ______ query injection appends a second complete statement after a semicolon (for example a SELECT followed by a separate DROP), when the database driver allows multiple statements in one call.

explanation.correct: Stacked (batched) queries chain a second standalone statement after a semicolon; if the driver executes multiple statements, this lets an attacker run entirely new commands.
explanation.exam_pattern: Second full statement after a semicolon = stacked (batched) queries.

questions.stem: Which WPA2 attack manipulates the 4-way handshake to force a client to reinstall an already-in-use key (an all-zero key), allowing decryption of traffic - without recovering the Wi-Fi password?

explanation.correct: KRACK replays handshake message 3 so the client reinstalls a used key (resetting nonces), enabling traffic decryption/forgery; it is a flaw in the WPA2 standard, fixed by patching clients.

distractors.A: An evil twin is a rogue AP impersonating an SSID, not a handshake key-reinstallation flaw.
distractors.B: A deauth flood disconnects clients; KRACK instead abuses the handshake to reinstall a key.
distractors.C: WPS PIN brute force recovers the passphrase via the weak WPS PIN, a different weakness.

explanation.exam_pattern: WPA2 handshake key reinstallation (all-zero key), no password recovery = KRACK.

references: CEH v13 Module 16: Hacking Wireless Networks

questions.stem: Driving around an area with a Wi-Fi adapter and GPS to discover, locate, and map wireless networks and their security settings is known as?

explanation.correct: Wardriving surveys and maps Wi-Fi networks (often with GPS) while moving through an area, building a picture of SSIDs, locations, and encryption in use.

distractors.A: Bluesnarfing steals data over Bluetooth; it is not Wi-Fi discovery by driving around.
distractors.C: An evil twin is a rogue AP impersonating a legitimate SSID, not a mapping technique.
distractors.D: War dialing scans ranges of phone numbers for modems/systems, not Wi-Fi mapping.

explanation.exam_pattern: Drive around mapping Wi-Fi networks with GPS = wardriving.

references: CEH v13 Module 16: Hacking Wireless Networks

questions.stem: Which Bluetooth attack involves stealing data - contacts, messages, or files - from a vulnerable device over its Bluetooth connection?

explanation.correct: Bluesnarfing is the unauthorized theft of data (contacts, messages, files) from a device over Bluetooth, exploiting weak pairing or implementation flaws.

distractors.B: Bluebugging takes control of a device's functions (e.g., calls); its hallmark is control, not data theft.
distractors.C: Bluejacking sends unsolicited messages to a device; it does not steal data from it.
distractors.D: An evil twin is a rogue Wi-Fi access point, not a Bluetooth attack.

explanation.exam_pattern: Steal data over Bluetooth = bluesnarfing; send spam = bluejacking; control the device = bluebugging.

references: CEH v13 Module 16: Hacking Wireless Networks

questions.stem: Which Wi-Fi deployment authenticates each user individually against a RADIUS server using 802.1X/EAP, instead of everyone sharing one pre-shared key?

explanation.correct: WPA2-Enterprise uses 802.1X/EAP with a RADIUS server so each user authenticates with unique credentials; revoking one user does not require changing a shared key for everyone.

distractors.B: WPA2-Personal uses a single shared pre-shared key for all clients, not per-user RADIUS auth.
distractors.C: An open network provides no authentication or encryption at all.
distractors.D: WEP is broken legacy encryption with no per-user 802.1X authentication of this kind.

explanation.exam_pattern: Per-user 802.1X/EAP via RADIUS = WPA2-Enterprise; shared key = WPA2-Personal.

references: CEH v13 Module 16: Hacking Wireless Networks

questions.stem: Fill in the blank: Hiding a wireless network by disabling ______ broadcast provides only weak security, because the network name is still revealed in client probe and association frames.

explanation.correct: Disabling SSID broadcast merely stops beacon advertisement; the SSID still appears in probe requests/responses and association frames, so a sniffer recovers it - it is obscurity, not security.
explanation.exam_pattern: Hiding the network name (disable SSID broadcast) is weak obscurity, not real security.

references: CEH v13 Module 16: Hacking Wireless Networks

questions.stem: Which mobile-app defense hard-codes the expected server certificate or public key so that a man-in-the-middle presenting a different (even validly signed) certificate is rejected?

explanation.correct: Certificate (or public-key) pinning makes the app trust only a specific certificate/key, so an interception proxy with a different cert is refused - a strong anti-MITM control for mobile apps.

distractors.A: Rooting removes Android restrictions; it does not pin certificates.
distractors.C: Sideloading installs apps outside the official store - a risk, not a TLS defense.
distractors.D: Jailbreaking removes iOS restrictions; it weakens security rather than defending against MITM.

explanation.exam_pattern: App trusts only a specific pinned cert/key to stop MITM = certificate pinning.

references: CEH v13 Module 17: Hacking Mobile Platforms

questions.stem: An attacker takes a legitimate Android app, inserts malicious code, and redistributes the modified package through third-party stores. Which mobile threat is this?

explanation.correct: App repackaging rebuilds a trusted app with added malware and distributes it (often via third-party stores), tricking users who think they are installing the legitimate app.

distractors.A: Containerization separates work and personal data - a defense, not this threat.
distractors.C: MDM is an enterprise management platform, not a repackaging attack.
distractors.D: Certificate pinning is a defensive control, not an attack that trojanizes an app.

explanation.exam_pattern: Trojanize a legit app and redistribute it = app repackaging.

references: CEH v13 Module 17: Hacking Mobile Platforms

questions.stem: A hidden app secretly installed on a target's phone to monitor their location, messages, and calls (sometimes sold as 'stalkerware') is best classified as which type of mobile malware?

explanation.correct: Such stalkerware is spyware: it covertly collects personal data (location, messages, calls) and reports it to the attacker, violating the victim's privacy.

distractors.B: Ransomware encrypts data and demands payment; it does not quietly monitor the user.
distractors.C: A rootkit hides presence to maintain access; covert data collection defines spyware here.
distractors.D: Adware pushes unwanted advertisements rather than covertly surveilling the user.

explanation.exam_pattern: Covertly monitor location/messages/calls = mobile spyware (stalkerware).

references: CEH v13 Module 17: Hacking Mobile Platforms

questions.stem: Fill in the blank: On employee-owned (BYOD) phones, enterprises separate corporate apps and data from personal data using ______, so a remote wipe can remove only the company's data.

explanation.correct: Containerization creates an isolated, managed 'work profile' on the device, letting the organization enforce policy and selectively wipe corporate data without touching personal content.
explanation.exam_pattern: Separate work and personal data for selective wipe on BYOD = containerization.

references: CEH v13 Module 17: Hacking Mobile Platforms

questions.stem: Which infamous IoT botnet spread by scanning the Internet for devices with open Telnet and trying a built-in list of factory-default logins, then used them to launch massive DDoS attacks?

explanation.correct: Mirai enslaved IoT devices (cameras, routers) by trying default Telnet credentials, then launched record DDoS attacks; changing default credentials and disabling Telnet are the fixes.

distractors.A: Stuxnet was a targeted ICS/SCADA worm against centrifuges, not a Telnet-default IoT botnet.
distractors.B: WannaCry was ransomware spread via an SMB exploit, not an IoT default-credential botnet.
distractors.C: Heartbleed was an OpenSSL memory-disclosure vulnerability, not a botnet.

explanation.exam_pattern: IoT botnet via default Telnet logins for DDoS = Mirai.

references: CEH v13 Module 18: IoT and OT Hacking

questions.stem: Which lightweight, RESTful IoT protocol runs over UDP for constrained devices and, lacking built-in authentication, relies on DTLS for security when exposed?

explanation.correct: CoAP is a RESTful, HTTP-like protocol over UDP for constrained IoT devices; it has no built-in authentication, so DTLS is used to secure it, and exposed CoAP servers can leak resources.

distractors.A: Zigbee is a low-power mesh radio standard, not a RESTful UDP application protocol.
distractors.C: Modbus is a legacy industrial (OT) protocol, not a RESTful UDP IoT protocol.
distractors.D: MQTT is a TCP-based publish/subscribe protocol using a broker, not a RESTful UDP protocol.

explanation.exam_pattern: RESTful UDP protocol for constrained IoT, secured by DTLS = CoAP.

references: CEH v13 Module 18: IoT and OT Hacking

questions.stem: Which reference model segments industrial control system (OT) networks into hierarchical levels - from the physical process up to enterprise IT - to guide where security zones and conduits belong?

options.text: The Purdue model (Purdue Enterprise Reference Architecture)

explanation.correct: The Purdue model organizes ICS/OT into hierarchical levels (physical process up to enterprise), guiding segmentation into zones and conduits between IT and OT.

distractors.A: The Cyber Kill Chain describes attack phases, not OT network segmentation.
distractors.C: STRIDE is a threat-modeling taxonomy, not an ICS reference architecture.
distractors.D: The OSI model describes seven networking layers generally; it is not an ICS segmentation model.

explanation.exam_pattern: Hierarchical ICS/OT segmentation model (process up to enterprise) = the Purdue model.

references: CEH v13 Module 18: IoT and OT Hacking

questions.stem: In an OT environment, which device directly controls physical equipment such as motors, pumps, and valves, making it a prime target because compromising it affects the physical process itself?

explanation.correct: A PLC executes control logic that drives field equipment (motors, valves), so compromising it can directly disrupt or damage the physical process - a high-impact OT target.

distractors.A: An enterprise router forwards IT traffic; it is not the controller of physical OT equipment.
distractors.B: A historian stores process data for analysis; it does not control field devices.
distractors.D: An HMI is the operator's screen for monitoring/control; it does not itself drive the equipment logic.

explanation.exam_pattern: Device executing control logic that drives physical equipment = PLC (prime OT target).

references: CEH v13 Module 18: IoT and OT Hacking

questions.stem: An attacker exploits an SSRF flaw in a cloud virtual machine to query the instance metadata service and steal the VM's temporary IAM credentials. Which component was the target?

explanation.correct: The instance metadata service returns a VM's identity and temporary role credentials; an SSRF that reaches it can exfiltrate those credentials. Enforcing the hardened/session-token metadata mode mitigates it.

distractors.A: A CASB brokers user-to-cloud access policy; it is not the metadata endpoint being abused.
distractors.B: A WAF filters inbound web attacks; it is a control, not the component that stores VM role credentials.
distractors.D: The hypervisor is provider-managed infrastructure, not the endpoint an SSRF queries for VM credentials.

explanation.exam_pattern: SSRF -> instance metadata service -> steal temporary IAM credentials.

questions.stem: A vulnerability lets a process break out of its container and gain access to the host operating system or other containers on the same host. Which risk is this?

explanation.correct: A container escape breaks the isolation boundary, giving the attacker the host or neighboring containers; it is a top container-security concern, mitigated by least privilege, no --privileged, and patching the runtime.

distractors.B: A collision attack finds two inputs with the same hash; it is a cryptographic attack, not container breakout.
distractors.C: Credential stuffing replays leaked credentials; it is not a container-isolation failure.
distractors.D: DNS poisoning corrupts resolver caches; it is unrelated to container isolation.

explanation.exam_pattern: Break out of a container to the host/other containers = container escape.

questions.stem: Which class of tool continuously scans cloud accounts for misconfigurations - public storage buckets, open security groups, overly broad IAM - and checks them against security benchmarks?

explanation.correct: CSPM continuously assesses cloud configuration against best-practice benchmarks and flags misconfigurations (public buckets, open ports, risky IAM), which are leading causes of cloud breaches.

distractors.A: A WAF filters web-application attacks; it does not audit cloud account configuration.
distractors.C: A SIEM aggregates and correlates logs; posture misconfiguration scanning is CSPM's role.
distractors.D: A CASB governs user-to-cloud access and visibility (shadow IT); it is not primarily a config-posture scanner.

explanation.exam_pattern: Continuously audit cloud config for misconfiguration = CSPM (vs CASB for access/visibility).

questions.stem: Fill in the blank: The open-source platform ______ automates the deployment, scaling, and management of containers, and its exposed API server or dashboard is a common cloud attack target.

explanation.correct: Kubernetes (K8s) orchestrates containers at scale; a misconfigured or exposed API server, kubelet, or dashboard can let an attacker deploy workloads or access secrets, so it must be locked down.
explanation.exam_pattern: Container orchestration platform (exposed API server is a target) = Kubernetes.

questions.stem: Which algorithm lets two parties who have never met securely agree on a shared secret over an untrusted channel, without ever transmitting the secret itself?

explanation.correct: Diffie-Hellman lets two parties derive a shared secret from exchanged public values, so the secret itself never crosses the wire - the basis of key exchange in many secure protocols.

distractors.A: SHA-256 is a one-way hash for integrity; it cannot establish a shared secret.
distractors.B: AES is a symmetric cipher that uses a key both sides already share; it does not negotiate one.
distractors.C: MD5 is a (now weak) hash function, not a key-agreement algorithm.

explanation.exam_pattern: Agree on a shared secret over an untrusted channel = Diffie-Hellman key exchange.

questions.stem: Which technique deliberately makes password hashing slow and resource-intensive (using many iterations or memory-hard functions like bcrypt, scrypt, or PBKDF2) to make brute-force and rainbow-table attacks far costlier?

explanation.correct: Key stretching applies a slow or memory-hard function (bcrypt/scrypt/PBKDF2) so each guess costs much more, blunting brute-force and precomputed attacks; it is typically combined with per-password salts.

distractors.A: Steganography hides data in a carrier; it is unrelated to slowing password hashing.
distractors.B: Salting adds uniqueness to defeat precomputed tables but does not by itself make each guess slow.
distractors.D: Tokenization substitutes a surrogate value for sensitive data; it is not a password-hashing hardener.

explanation.exam_pattern: Make hashing deliberately slow/memory-hard (bcrypt/scrypt/PBKDF2) = key stretching (pair with salt).

questions.stem: Which of the following is an ASYMMETRIC algorithm, used for key exchange or digital signatures rather than bulk symmetric encryption?

explanation.correct: RSA is an asymmetric algorithm (public/private key pair) used for key transport and digital signatures; ECC and Diffie-Hellman are other asymmetric examples.

distractors.A: AES is a symmetric block cipher using one shared key.
distractors.B: 3DES is a symmetric block cipher (triple DES), not asymmetric.
distractors.D: RC4 is a symmetric stream cipher, now deprecated.

explanation.exam_pattern: Asymmetric = RSA/ECC/Diffie-Hellman; symmetric = AES/3DES/RC4/Blowfish.

questions.stem: Which PKI mechanism lets a client check, in real time, whether a single specific certificate has been revoked, instead of downloading and searching a full list of revoked certificates?

explanation.correct: OCSP queries the responder for the status of one certificate in real time, avoiding the overhead of downloading a whole CRL; OCSP stapling lets the server present a signed status to clients.

distractors.A: A CSR is the request submitted to obtain a certificate; it does not check revocation.
distractors.B: A CRL is the full, periodically published list of revoked certificates the client must download and search.
distractors.D: The CA issues and signs certificates; checking revocation status is done via OCSP or a CRL.

explanation.exam_pattern: Real-time status of ONE cert = OCSP; the full downloaded list = CRL.

questions.stem: An attacker tries every entry from a prepared list of likely passwords against a login prompt. Which password attack is this?

explanation.correct: A dictionary attack tries candidates from a curated wordlist of likely passwords, making it faster than exhausting every combination.

distractors.A: A rainbow table attack reverses captured hashes using precomputed tables, not live guessing.
distractors.C: A brute-force attack systematically tries all possible character combinations, not a wordlist.
distractors.D: Pass-the-hash reuses a stolen hash to authenticate; it does not guess plaintext passwords.

explanation.exam_pattern: Curated wordlist of likely passwords = dictionary attack.

questions.stem: Which password-cracking method relies on large precomputed tables that map hashes back to their plaintext, trading disk space for cracking speed?

explanation.correct: A rainbow table attack uses precomputed hash-to-plaintext chains, so cracking a captured hash becomes a fast lookup instead of hashing candidates at attack time.

distractors.A: A dictionary attack hashes each wordlist candidate during the attack; it stores no precomputed tables.
distractors.B: Online brute-force guesses against the live service and is slow and noisy.
distractors.D: Password spraying tries a few common passwords across many accounts to avoid lockout.

explanation.exam_pattern: Precomputed hash-to-plaintext tables = rainbow tables (salting defeats them).

questions.stem: Which defensive technique adds a unique random value to each password before hashing, most directly defeating precomputed rainbow-table attacks?

explanation.correct: Salting adds a unique random value per password, so identical passwords hash differently and a single precomputed table cannot be reused - defeating rainbow tables.

distractors.A: Lockout slows online guessing but does nothing against offline precomputed-table lookups.
distractors.B: Length raises brute-force cost but does not stop a precomputed table from matching a given hash.
distractors.D: Single sign-on centralizes authentication; it does not protect stored hashes from rainbow tables.

explanation.exam_pattern: Unique random value per password that breaks precomputed tables = salting.

questions.stem: An attacker captures an NTLM password hash and authenticates to other systems using the hash itself, without ever cracking the plaintext password. What is this technique?

explanation.correct: Pass-the-hash reuses a captured NTLM hash directly to authenticate, so the attacker never needs the cleartext password.

distractors.A: Credential stuffing replays leaked username/password pairs, not hashes, against logins.
distractors.B: Password spraying guesses a few common passwords across many accounts.
distractors.C: Kerberoasting requests service tickets to crack service-account passwords offline, a different flow.

explanation.exam_pattern: Authenticate with the hash itself, no cracking = pass-the-hash.

questions.stem: After gaining a standard-user shell, an attacker exploits a misconfiguration to obtain SYSTEM/root-level rights on the same host. What is this step called?

explanation.correct: Raising one's rights from a limited account to administrative/root level is privilege escalation (vertical escalation).

distractors.A: Footprinting is early information gathering, not gaining higher rights.
distractors.C: Banner grabbing reads service versions; it does not elevate privileges.
distractors.D: Lateral movement spreads to other hosts at a similar privilege, not higher rights on the same host.

explanation.exam_pattern: Higher rights on the same host = (vertical) privilege escalation; other hosts = lateral movement.

questions.stem: An insider hides a confidential spreadsheet inside an ordinary-looking JPEG image so the data can leave the network without drawing attention. Which technique is this?

explanation.correct: Steganography conceals the existence of data by embedding it inside a carrier file such as an image, so the hidden content is not obvious.

distractors.A: Hashing is a one-way digest; it cannot hide and later recover a file inside another.
distractors.B: Tokenization substitutes a surrogate value for sensitive data; it does not hide a file in a carrier.
distractors.C: Encryption scrambles data but produces visible ciphertext, revealing that something is protected.

explanation.exam_pattern: Hide data's existence inside a carrier (image/audio) = steganography; scramble it = cryptography.

questions.stem: Fill in the blank: Deleting or altering a system's security and event ______ is a common way attackers cover their tracks and hide evidence of an intrusion.

explanation.correct: Clearing or tampering with logs removes the record of attacker activity; forwarding logs to a secured, centralized server defends against this covering-tracks technique.
explanation.exam_pattern: Hide intrusion evidence by clearing/altering logs = covering tracks.

questions.stem: Which TWO tools are primarily offline password-hash crackers used after the hashes have already been obtained? (Choose two.)

explanation.correct: Hashcat and John the Ripper both crack captured password hashes offline using dictionary, brute-force, and rule-based attacks.

distractors.B: Wireshark is a packet capture and analysis tool, not a hash cracker.
distractors.D: Nikto is a web-server vulnerability scanner, not a password cracker.

explanation.exam_pattern: Crack captured hashes offline = Hashcat / John the Ripper.

questions.stem: Which type of malware self-replicates and spreads across networks on its own, without attaching to a host file or requiring a user to run it?

explanation.correct: A worm is self-replicating and self-propagating; it spreads across networks without a host file or user action.

distractors.A: A virus attaches to a host file and needs that file to be executed to spread.
distractors.C: A Trojan masquerades as legitimate software and does not self-replicate.
distractors.D: A rootkit hides presence on a system; it does not self-propagate across a network.

explanation.exam_pattern: Self-spreading with no host file/user action = worm; needs a host file = virus.

questions.stem: A user installs a 'free game' that secretly opens a backdoor giving an attacker remote control of the machine. Which malware category best fits?

explanation.correct: Software disguised as something desirable that hides a malicious payload is a Trojan; one that grants remote control is a RAT.

distractors.A: Ransomware encrypts files and demands payment; it is not primarily a hidden remote-control tool.
distractors.B: A worm self-propagates and is not disguised as a wanted application.
distractors.D: Adware displays unwanted advertisements rather than granting remote control.

explanation.exam_pattern: Disguised-as-legit plus hidden payload = Trojan; remote-control backdoor = RAT.

questions.stem: Which malware is specifically designed to conceal its own presence and that of other malicious components, often by subverting the operating-system kernel?

explanation.correct: A rootkit hides files, processes, and itself (sometimes at kernel level) to maintain stealthy, privileged access.

distractors.B: A keylogger records keystrokes; concealment is not its defining purpose.
distractors.C: A worm spreads to other hosts rather than hiding on one.
distractors.D: Ransomware announces itself by encrypting files and demanding payment, the opposite of hiding.

explanation.exam_pattern: Stealth and self-concealment, often kernel-level = rootkit.

questions.stem: Malware encrypts a victim's files and demands payment in exchange for the decryption key. Which category is this?

explanation.correct: Ransomware encrypts data and extorts the victim for the key; offline, tested backups are the primary defense.

distractors.A: A logic bomb triggers a payload when a condition is met; encryption-for-ransom is not its definition.
distractors.B: Spyware covertly collects information rather than encrypting data for ransom.
distractors.C: A rootkit hides presence; it does not encrypt files for extortion.

explanation.exam_pattern: Encrypt files and demand payment = ransomware.

questions.stem: A well-resourced group quietly maintains long-term access to a target network to steal data over many months while avoiding detection. This is best described as a(n)?

explanation.correct: An APT is a stealthy, well-resourced actor that maintains long-term, persistent access to exfiltrate data over an extended period.

distractors.B: A worm outbreak is noisy and automated, not quiet long-term access.
distractors.C: Script kiddies lack the sophistication and sustained persistence described.
distractors.D: A drive-by download is a single infection vector, not a months-long campaign.

explanation.exam_pattern: Stealthy, well-funded, long-term persistent access = APT.

questions.stem: An analyst runs a suspicious binary inside an isolated sandbox and observes the files, registry keys, and network connections it creates. Which malware-analysis approach is this?

explanation.correct: Dynamic analysis executes the sample in a controlled sandbox and observes its runtime behavior - file, registry, and network activity.

distractors.A: Static analysis inspects the file without executing it (strings, headers, disassembly).
distractors.C: Differential cryptanalysis attacks ciphers, not the behavior of a program.
distractors.D: Steganalysis detects data hidden inside carrier files; it is not malware behavior analysis.

explanation.exam_pattern: Run it and observe behavior = dynamic; inspect without running = static.

questions.stem: Fill in the blank: Examining a malware sample's strings, headers, imports, and disassembly without executing it is called ______ analysis.

explanation.correct: Static analysis inspects the file's contents without running it, so the code never executes and the examination carries no risk of infection.
explanation.exam_pattern: Inspect the sample without executing it = static analysis.

questions.stem: Thousands of compromised 'zombie' hosts take orders from a command-and-control server to launch attacks on demand. This network of bots is called a?

explanation.correct: A botnet is a network of compromised hosts (bots/zombies) controlled through a command-and-control channel to carry out coordinated attacks such as DDoS or spam.

distractors.A: A Faraday cage blocks radio signals; it is unrelated to compromised hosts.
distractors.C: A honeynet is a decoy network set up by defenders to study attackers.
distractors.D: A rainbow table is a password-cracking data structure, not a network of hosts.

explanation.exam_pattern: Zombies plus command-and-control = botnet.

questions.stem: Which tool is purpose-built to scan web servers for thousands of known dangerous files, outdated server versions, and common misconfigurations?

explanation.correct: Nikto is a web-server scanner that checks for thousands of risky files/CGIs, outdated software, and server misconfigurations.

distractors.A: Aircrack-ng cracks wireless encryption keys; it does not scan web servers.
distractors.B: Responder poisons LLMNR/NBT-NS to capture hashes; it is not a web-server scanner.
distractors.D: John the Ripper is an offline password cracker, not a web-server scanner.

explanation.exam_pattern: Scan a web server for known bad files/versions/misconfigs = Nikto.

references: CEH v13 Module 13: Hacking Web Servers

questions.stem: By requesting a URL that contains sequences like ../../ an attacker reads files outside the web root, such as the system password file. Which web-server attack is this?

explanation.correct: Directory (path) traversal uses ../ sequences to escape the web root and access files the server should not expose.

distractors.A: ARP poisoning redirects LAN traffic; it does not read server files via a URL.
distractors.B: A deauthentication attack disconnects Wi-Fi clients; it is unrelated to web paths.
distractors.D: A SYN flood is a denial-of-service technique, not file access via path manipulation.

explanation.exam_pattern: ../ sequences to escape the web root and read arbitrary files = directory/path traversal.

references: CEH v13 Module 13: Hacking Web Servers

questions.stem: An organization keeps getting compromised through publicly known vulnerabilities in its outdated web-server software. Which practice most directly addresses this root cause?

explanation.correct: Known vulnerabilities in outdated software are closed by applying vendor patches promptly, so disciplined patch management is the direct remedy.

distractors.A: Disabling ICMP neither patches nor mitigates the underlying software flaw.
distractors.C: Longer passwords do not fix a code vulnerability in the server software.
distractors.D: Adding RAM is a performance measure, not a vulnerability remediation.

explanation.exam_pattern: Repeated compromise via known flaws in old software = fix with patch/update management.

references: CEH v13 Module 13: Hacking Web Servers

questions.stem: During hardening, which misconfiguration should be addressed first because attackers routinely try it against newly exposed web servers and admin consoles?

explanation.correct: Default/unchanged admin credentials are trivially guessed and widely documented, so they are a top-priority hardening fix.

distractors.A: Serving over HTTPS is a good practice, not a misconfiguration to fix.
distractors.B: Minified JavaScript is a normal optimization, not a security misconfiguration.
distractors.C: HTML comments can leak minor information but are far lower risk than default admin logins.

explanation.exam_pattern: Change default/admin credentials first - they are attackers' easiest win.

references: CEH v13 Module 13: Hacking Web Servers

questions.stem: Fill in the blank: Configuring a web server to suppress its detailed product and version in the HTTP Server response ______ reduces the information an attacker gains from banner grabbing.

explanation.correct: The Server response header can reveal the exact web-server product and version; suppressing or genericizing it limits footprinting (defense in depth, not a fix for any underlying flaw).
explanation.exam_pattern: Hide the web-server version in the Server header to reduce footprinting.

references: CEH v13 Module 13: Hacking Web Servers

questions.stem: An attacker submits a comment containing a script; every visitor who later views that comment has the script run in their browser. Which attack and variant is this?

explanation.correct: The script is saved on the server and served to every viewer, which is stored (persistent) XSS.

distractors.B: SQL injection targets the database, not script execution in each visitor's browser.
distractors.C: CSRF forces a state-changing action using the victim's session; it does not plant a persistent script.
distractors.D: Reflected XSS runs from a crafted request/link and is not stored server-side for all users.

explanation.exam_pattern: Script saved server-side and served to all viewers = stored XSS; echoed from a request = reflected.

references: CEH v13 Module 14: Hacking Web Applications

questions.stem: A search page echoes the user's query straight back into the HTML. An attacker emails a crafted link that runs script in the victim's browser only when the victim clicks it. Which variant is this?

explanation.correct: The payload is reflected back from the request and executes when the victim follows the crafted link, which is reflected XSS.

distractors.A: Clickjacking tricks a user into clicking a hidden element; it does not echo script from a request.
distractors.C: 'DOM-based SQL injection' is not a real category; it mixes unrelated terms.
distractors.D: Stored XSS persists on the server and affects all viewers, not only one who clicks a link.

explanation.exam_pattern: Payload echoed from the request (crafted link) = reflected XSS; persisted server-side = stored.

references: CEH v13 Module 14: Hacking Web Applications

questions.stem: A logged-in user visits a malicious page that silently submits a form to their bank's 'transfer funds' endpoint, abusing the user's existing authenticated session. Which attack is this?

explanation.correct: CSRF rides the victim's existing authenticated session to force a state-changing request the user did not intend; anti-CSRF tokens are the standard defense.

distractors.B: Brute-force login guesses credentials; the user here is already authenticated.
distractors.C: Reflected XSS executes script; here the attack forces a request using the user's session.
distractors.D: Directory traversal reads files on the server, not forged user actions.

explanation.exam_pattern: Force a state-changing request using the victim's active session = CSRF (anti-CSRF tokens defend).

references: CEH v13 Module 14: Hacking Web Applications

questions.stem: Which tool acts as an intercepting proxy, letting a tester view and modify HTTP requests between the browser and a web application?

explanation.correct: Burp Suite (like OWASP ZAP) sits between the browser and the app as an intercepting proxy, so requests and responses can be inspected and tampered with.

distractors.A: Nmap scans ports and services; it is not a web proxy.
distractors.C: Hashcat cracks password hashes; it does not proxy HTTP.
distractors.D: Wireshark passively captures packets but is not an inline HTTP proxy for editing requests.

explanation.exam_pattern: Intercept and modify HTTP requests to a web app = Burp Suite (or OWASP ZAP).

references: CEH v13 Module 14: Hacking Web Applications

questions.stem: By changing an 'account_id' value in a URL, a user views another customer's records because the app never checks ownership. Which OWASP Top 10 category does this fall under?

explanation.correct: Reaching another user's data by tampering with an object reference and no ownership check is an insecure direct object reference (IDOR), a form of broken access control.

distractors.A: Security misconfiguration is about insecure settings/defaults, not a missing authorization check.
distractors.B: Cryptographic failures involve weak or missing encryption, not access-control gaps.
distractors.D: Vulnerable and outdated components concern unpatched libraries, not this ownership-check flaw.

explanation.exam_pattern: Change an object reference to reach data you shouldn't = IDOR, under broken access control.

references: CEH v13 Module 14: Hacking Web Applications

questions.stem: Which community-maintained awareness document ranks the ten most critical web application security risks and is widely used to prioritize testing and remediation?

explanation.correct: The OWASP Top 10 is a community awareness document ranking the ten most critical web application security risks, guiding testing priorities.

distractors.B: The CVE list enumerates specific disclosed vulnerabilities; it is not a ranked web-risk document.
distractors.C: CIS benchmarks are configuration baselines, not a ranked list of web application risks.
distractors.D: NIST SP 800-53 is a broad security and privacy control catalog, not a web-app top ten.

explanation.exam_pattern: Ten most critical web app risks = OWASP Top 10.

references: CEH v13 Module 14: Hacking Web Applications

questions.stem: An attacker enters ' OR '1'='1 into a login field and the application concatenates it directly into a database query, changing the query's logic. Which vulnerability class is this?

explanation.correct: Untrusted input altering the structure of a SQL query is SQL injection, which can bypass authentication or expose data.

distractors.A: Clickjacking overlays UI to hijack clicks; it does not alter database queries.
distractors.B: Session fixation forces a known session ID; it is unrelated to query manipulation.
distractors.D: XSS injects script that runs in the browser, not SQL that runs in the database.

explanation.exam_pattern: Untrusted input altering a SQL query = SQL injection.

questions.stem: Which TWO are forms of SQL injection in which the attacker infers data indirectly rather than seeing it returned directly in the response? (Choose two.)

explanation.correct: Blind SQL injection infers data indirectly: boolean-based reads true/false differences in responses, and time-based reads deliberate response delays.

distractors.B: UNION-based injection returns data directly in the application's output (in-band).
distractors.C: Error-based injection reveals data through returned database error messages (in-band).

explanation.exam_pattern: Inferential/blind SQLi = boolean-based and time-based; in-band = UNION-based and error-based.

questions.stem: An attacker appends a UNION SELECT to a vulnerable query to pull columns from another table into the application's normal results. Which type of SQL injection is this?

explanation.correct: Using UNION SELECT to merge another table's data into the displayed results is UNION-based, an in-band technique because the data appears directly in the response.

distractors.A: Boolean-based blind injection infers data from true/false behavior, not from merged visible output.
distractors.B: Reflected XSS executes script in the browser; it is not SQL injection.
distractors.D: DOM-based XSS is a client-side script flaw, not a SQL technique.

explanation.exam_pattern: UNION SELECT to merge another table into visible output = UNION-based (in-band) SQLi.

questions.stem: Which coding practice most effectively prevents SQL injection by separating code from data so user input is never interpreted as part of the SQL command?

explanation.correct: Parameterized queries/prepared statements bind user input as data, so it can never change the query structure - the primary SQL injection defense (with input validation).

distractors.A: Encoding input does not prevent injection and can be decoded before the query runs.
distractors.C: Hiding the version banner is obscurity; it does not stop injection.
distractors.D: Client-side limits are trivially bypassed by sending requests directly to the server.

explanation.exam_pattern: Prepared statements / parameterized queries (plus input validation) = primary SQLi defense.

questions.stem: Fill in the blank: The open-source tool ______ automates the detection and exploitation of SQL injection flaws and the extraction of database contents during authorized testing.

explanation.correct: sqlmap automates discovering and leveraging SQL injection points and dumping database data; in a CEH context it is used only under explicit authorization.
explanation.exam_pattern: Automated SQL injection detection/extraction tool = sqlmap.

questions.stem: Which legacy wireless security protocol is considered broken because its use of RC4 with weak initialization vectors lets an attacker recover the key after capturing enough traffic?

explanation.correct: WEP's RC4 stream cipher with short, reused initialization vectors leaks key material, so captured traffic allows key recovery - WEP is deprecated.

distractors.A: EAP-TLS is an enterprise authentication method, not the broken legacy encryption protocol.
distractors.C: WPA2 uses AES-CCMP and is far stronger than WEP.
distractors.D: WPA3 is the newest and strongest Wi-Fi security standard.

explanation.exam_pattern: RC4 plus weak IVs, recoverable key = WEP (deprecated).

references: CEH v13 Module 16: Hacking Wireless Networks

questions.stem: Which Wi-Fi security standard replaces the WPA2 pre-shared-key handshake with Simultaneous Authentication of Equals (SAE) to resist offline dictionary attacks?

explanation.correct: WPA3 introduces SAE (the dragonfly handshake), which resists offline dictionary attacks against the captured handshake, unlike WPA2's PSK exchange.

distractors.A: An open network provides no authentication or encryption at all.
distractors.B: WEP has no such handshake and is fundamentally broken.
distractors.C: WPA with TKIP predates SAE and is also deprecated.

explanation.exam_pattern: SAE (dragonfly) handshake resisting offline cracking = WPA3.

references: CEH v13 Module 16: Hacking Wireless Networks

questions.stem: Which tool suite is commonly used to capture wireless frames and crack WEP/WPA pre-shared keys during authorized wireless assessments?

explanation.correct: Aircrack-ng captures 802.11 frames and performs WEP/WPA key cracking, the standard suite for authorized Wi-Fi testing.

distractors.A: sqlmap targets SQL injection in web apps.
distractors.C: Nikto scans web servers, not wireless networks.
distractors.D: Burp Suite is a web intercepting proxy, not a wireless cracking suite.

explanation.exam_pattern: Capture Wi-Fi frames and crack WEP/WPA keys = Aircrack-ng.

references: CEH v13 Module 16: Hacking Wireless Networks

questions.stem: An attacker sets up a rogue access point broadcasting the same SSID as a legitimate corporate network to lure clients into connecting through the attacker. Which attack is this?

explanation.correct: An evil twin is a rogue AP impersonating a legitimate SSID so victims associate with it, enabling interception of their traffic.

distractors.A: SQL injection is a web/database attack, unrelated to wireless association.
distractors.B: A Smurf attack is an ICMP amplification denial-of-service.
distractors.D: MAC flooding overflows a switch's CAM table on a wired LAN, not a rogue Wi-Fi AP.

explanation.exam_pattern: Rogue AP cloning a legitimate SSID to intercept clients = evil twin.

references: CEH v13 Module 16: Hacking Wireless Networks

questions.stem: To force a client off the network so it reconnects - letting the attacker capture the WPA2 four-way handshake - an attacker floods it with spoofed 802.11 management frames. Which attack is this?

explanation.correct: A deauthentication attack sends spoofed 802.11 deauth management frames to disconnect clients; the forced reconnection lets the attacker capture the handshake for offline cracking.

distractors.A: A rainbow table attack cracks hashes offline; it does not disconnect clients.
distractors.B: ARP poisoning is a wired-LAN man-in-the-middle technique, not an 802.11 frame attack.
distractors.D: Phishing is social engineering, not a wireless frame flood.

explanation.exam_pattern: Spoofed 802.11 deauth frames to knock clients off / capture the handshake = deauthentication attack.

references: CEH v13 Module 16: Hacking Wireless Networks

questions.stem: Fill in the blank: Wi-Fi Protected Setup (______) is often disabled on access points because its 8-digit PIN can be brute-forced to recover the wireless passphrase.

explanation.correct: WPS was meant to simplify connecting devices, but its PIN is validated in two weak halves and can be brute-forced, so disabling WPS is a common hardening step.
explanation.exam_pattern: 8-digit PIN brute-forceable - disable it = WPS weakness.

references: CEH v13 Module 16: Hacking Wireless Networks

questions.stem: Removing the manufacturer's built-in restrictions on a mobile device to gain privileged (root/administrator) control is called jailbreaking on iOS and what on Android?

explanation.correct: Gaining privileged control by stripping vendor restrictions is rooting on Android (jailbreaking on iOS); it weakens the device's security model.

distractors.B: Tethering shares the device's connection with other devices.
distractors.C: Provisioning configures a device for enterprise management.
distractors.D: Sideloading installs apps from outside the official store - related risk, but a different action.

explanation.exam_pattern: Remove vendor restrictions for privileged control: jailbreak (iOS) / root (Android).

references: CEH v13 Module 17: Hacking Mobile Platforms

questions.stem: Which solution lets an enterprise enforce passcodes, push configuration profiles, and remotely wipe lost or stolen smartphones across its fleet?

explanation.correct: MDM (part of broader MDM/UEM) centrally enforces device policy, pushes configuration, and supports remote lock/wipe of managed devices.

distractors.A: A SIEM rule detects and correlates events but cannot enforce device policy or wipe a phone.
distractors.B: A rainbow table is a password-cracking data structure, not a management platform.
distractors.D: A honeypot is a decoy system, not a device-management tool.

explanation.exam_pattern: Enforce policy / remote-wipe a device fleet = MDM.

references: CEH v13 Module 17: Hacking Mobile Platforms

questions.stem: A user installs an app from an untrusted third-party source instead of the official app store, bypassing the store's vetting. Which practice (and risk) is this?

explanation.correct: Installing apps from outside the official store is sideloading, which skips store vetting and raises the chance of installing malware.

distractors.A: Containerization separates work and personal data - a defensive control, not this risk.
distractors.C: Tethering shares connectivity, not app installation.
distractors.D: Rooting removes OS restrictions; it is a different action from installing an outside app.

explanation.exam_pattern: Install apps outside the official store = sideloading (raises malware risk).

references: CEH v13 Module 17: Hacking Mobile Platforms

questions.stem: A mobile app stores authentication tokens in clear text in a world-readable file on the device. Which OWASP Mobile risk category does this best illustrate?

explanation.correct: Saving sensitive data unprotected on the device is insecure data storage, a core OWASP Mobile risk; secrets should use the platform keystore/keychain.

distractors.A: SQL injection targets server-side databases via untrusted input.
distractors.C: Reflected XSS is a web-application attack, not on-device storage.
distractors.D: Weak wireless encryption concerns the network link, not local file storage.

explanation.exam_pattern: Sensitive data saved unprotected on the device = insecure data storage (OWASP Mobile).

references: CEH v13 Module 17: Hacking Mobile Platforms

questions.stem: Fill in the blank: Mobile operating systems isolate each app and its data from other apps using an application ______, limiting the damage a malicious app can do.

explanation.correct: The application sandbox confines each app to its own resources and data, so a compromised or malicious app cannot freely reach other apps' data - a core mobile security control.
explanation.exam_pattern: Per-app isolation of code and data = application sandbox.

references: CEH v13 Module 17: Hacking Mobile Platforms

questions.stem: An assessor wants to locate Internet-exposed IoT devices and industrial systems by their service banners without scanning them directly. Which resource is most associated with this?

explanation.correct: Shodan indexes Internet-connected devices - including IoT and ICS/SCADA systems - so a tester can find exposed devices passively by banner.

distractors.B: Responder poisons LLMNR/NBT-NS on a local network; it does not discover Internet-exposed devices.
distractors.C: Aircrack-ng is a wireless cracking suite, not an Internet device index.
distractors.D: John the Ripper is an offline password cracker, not a device search engine.

explanation.exam_pattern: Find exposed IoT/ICS devices by banner = Shodan.

references: CEH v13 Module 18: IoT and OT Hacking

questions.stem: In operational technology (OT) environments, which legacy industrial protocol is known for lacking built-in authentication and encryption, making network segmentation essential?

explanation.correct: Modbus is a widely deployed ICS protocol that was designed without authentication or encryption, so isolating it with segmentation is a primary compensating control.

distractors.A: HTTPS provides encrypted, authenticated web transport - the opposite of the stated weakness.
distractors.C: TLS 1.3 is a modern secure transport protocol.
distractors.D: SSH provides authenticated, encrypted remote sessions.

explanation.exam_pattern: Legacy ICS protocol with no auth/encryption = Modbus (segment the OT network).

references: CEH v13 Module 18: IoT and OT Hacking

questions.stem: Which lightweight publish/subscribe messaging protocol is widely used by IoT devices and, if its broker is left unauthenticated, can expose device data to anyone who connects?

explanation.correct: MQTT is a lightweight publish/subscribe protocol common in IoT; an unauthenticated or unencrypted broker can leak device data, so TLS and authentication are needed.

distractors.A: LDAP is a directory-access protocol.
distractors.C: NTP is a time-synchronization protocol.
distractors.D: SMTP is an email transport protocol, not an IoT pub/sub protocol.

explanation.exam_pattern: Lightweight IoT pub/sub protocol = MQTT (secure the broker with TLS and auth).

references: CEH v13 Module 18: IoT and OT Hacking

questions.stem: Large IoT botnets have historically spread by logging into devices with well-known factory default usernames and passwords. Which single hardening step most directly stops this?

explanation.correct: IoT botnets like those that abused default logins are stopped at the source by replacing factory default credentials with strong, unique ones.

distractors.A: DHCP lease time has no bearing on default-credential abuse.
distractors.C: Channel width is a performance setting and does not affect default logins.
distractors.D: Enabling UPnP can increase exposure, not reduce it.

explanation.exam_pattern: IoT compromise via factory default logins = fix by changing default credentials.

references: CEH v13 Module 18: IoT and OT Hacking

questions.stem: Which TWO controls most directly reduce risk in an environment full of hard-to-patch IoT and OT devices? (Choose two.)

options.text: Exposing device management interfaces directly to the Internet
Network segmentation that isolates IoT/OT from general IT
Disabling all logging on the devices
Changing default credentials and disabling unused services

explanation.correct: Segmenting IoT/OT away from IT limits lateral movement, and removing default credentials plus unused services shrinks the attack surface - both are core mitigations when patching is hard.

distractors.A: Exposing management interfaces to the Internet greatly increases risk.
distractors.C: Disabling logging removes the visibility needed to detect attacks, helping attackers.

explanation.exam_pattern: Segment IoT/OT and remove default creds/unused services = core IoT/OT hardening.

references: CEH v13 Module 18: IoT and OT Hacking
